newsitem.title: USA: U.S. regulation strangling exchanges - NYMEX.
newsitem.headline: U.S. regulation strangling exchanges - NYMEX.

text.p: The Sumitomo scandal has dragged on COMEX's ability to sell the notion of futures markets to potential hedgers at the same time that regulation is threatening to strangle U.S. futures exchanges, said Robert Green, director of marketing in NYMEX's COMEX division.

"We are not in the business of reforming for LME (London Metal Exchange)," Green told delegates at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries Round Table here. "Rather our issue is with the disturbing direction of the U.S. regulatory environment which is inexorably tending to increase regulation of exchanges and leaving the over-the-counter market totally unregulated."
"Our point is that by putting LME (copper) warehouses on U.S. soil, the LME should be regulated," Green said. The LME opened copper warehouses in April 1995.

"But beyond that point, we as exchanges are being gradually strangulated and left to prey to our competition. The Chicago exchanges have a similar problem. This is a much broader issue than LME versus COMEX. This is an issue of survivial of futures exchanges," Green said.
Nevertheless, COMEX was studying several issues to raise the volume of dealings on the exchange even though the vast majority of pricing of copper sales in the United States was based on COMEX.
COMEX officials argue that if more players hedged on COMEX rather than just using the market as a reference price, the price would be even more representative of the U.S. market.
But Green admitted that traders say they can make more money on the LME than COMEX because of London's principal to principal style of trading.

The arrival of LME warehouses in the U.S. spelled the beginning of the end for COMEX copper, some had initially predicted. "We don't hear these comments anymore. The contract is alive and well and healthier than it has been for years," Green said.

COMEX was still studying the installation of warehouses outside the United States. "My own gut feeling it's probably a good idea," Green said. Some were, however, concerned that warehouses outside the U.S. may impact on COMEX's role as a domestic benchmark price.
"The decision has not been made but it's under very active study. They would not necessarily be in South America but could be in other places," Green said.
Green said although LME volumes were much larger than COMEX, "some of the London volume statistics are skewed by reporting short term carries. Our market is used a lot more than is shown by volume."

COMEX introduced strip calendar trading for copper from September 20, and its next aim was to begin jumbo or large "all or nothing" order trading, with a minimum of 40 lots or 500 tons bought or sold in one execution to attract large institutional investors.

But some delegates complained that innovations already introduced to boost volume, such as ACCESS electronic trading, lacked liquidity to be representative. Others noted that most players on COMEX dealt in small 5 to 10 ton lots at a time and the jumbo order would be too big for them to handle.
Even the launch of another aluminum contract was under study but Green felt it was less likely to happen.

Since the Sumitomo scandal, COMEX has taken no extra steps to protect its users, Green said. "Sumitomo did not trade on our market, and maybe they did that for a reason. Maybe the regulatory environment discouraged them which would tend to say the regulatory environment is sound and COMEX customers are protected."
